Additionally, the results show that models with more parameters tend to demonstrate more reliable performance and less variation, with a substantial 310% to 1040% improvement over the smaller models when using the respective evaluation datasets.

In this research, we have established stringent limitations on the parameter space of the Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model based on recent LHC findings. We've found discrepancies between this model's predicted cosmic properties and data, which could be attributed to a strong first-order phase transition. Various searches for Higgs bosons in this model show that it's difficult for this transition to be first-order. We've found the only areas not yet restricted by the LHC require low mass for the Higgs boson, which is 100-150 GeV, and a specific relationship between its coupling to b-quarks and other Higgs bosons. We've found this coupling is also relevant to future particle accelerator studies. We've found the region not yet restricted by the LHC is linked to baryogenesis through the electroweak transition. We've found this could be verified by looking for gravitational wave signals. We've found the model's predictions for low-mass Higgs bosons could be tested by looking for them decaying into pairs of bottom quarks. We've found this could be found by looking for anomalies in superposition flavor changing processes.

We have carried out an in-depth investigation of low-lying excitations within a square lattice Fermi-Hubbard system utilizing a quantum computer.  Our study, which involved an 18-qubit experiment utilizing open source software and superconducting transmon qubits, revealed that the observed low-lying excitations align with those derived from advanced many-body techniques used to analyze correlated systems.  Our results demonstrate that the lowest-lying excitations of Dirac spin liquid phases are particularly susceptible to the observed excitations, which according to theoretical frameworks, are predicted to lie just below a spin gap, within a pair of excitations characterized by monopole charges of +1 and -1, respectively, within the magnetization dualities of these correlated systems.  Our study successfully identified a low-lying dual excitation with monopole charges of +1 that lies within an experimentally determined range of the spin gap, which serves as a strong indication of the presence of Dirac spin liquid correlations within the observed excitations.  Our findings underscore the potential of current techniques in simulating advanced correlated spin states within the lattice system using current quantum computers, which may facilitate the discovery of novel spin correlations within experiments utilizing cold atoms in optical lattices in the future, which are utilized to simulate these correlated systems.

The breaking of symmetries in lattice systems is analyzed specifically in a model with no $Z_3$ symmetry, and the model's behavior under this anomaly is studied using both the Schwinger-Dyson equations and quantum Monte Carlo methods. Our findings indicate that as the number of temporal sites increases, the symmetry is broken more intensely, and these sites can be mapped to the effective Kondo model in the case of weak coupling. Furthermore, our simulations show that in a regime with zero coupling, the numerical results from Monte Carlo methods are consistent with Schwinger-Dyson equations, but diverge in all but the weak coupling regime, with the divergence being attributed to the divergence of the stochastic noise in Monte Carlo simulations.

A novel chemical approach involving the argon-fluorine plasma etching process reveals Cr$_2$Al single crystals. These crystals display order-disorder phase transitions and magnetic ordering, as well as interesting magnetic properties. Unlike Mn$_2$Au with its one-dimensional magnetic order, Cr$_2$Al exhibits a three-dimensional magnetic structure. Magnetic responses are observed in Cr$_2$Al, similar to those in Mn$_2$Au. Additionally, Cr$_2$Al single layers show a combination of ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic properties, manifesting as a ferri- and antiferrointerface.

A new model for calculating rarefied micro-flows has been developed, with an enhanced ability to simulate thermal transpiration at the canonical level. This model is based on a uniform gas model ($\nu$-model), built upon a generalized13-moment closure system. To improve thermal transpiration accuracy, both relaxation coefficients in this system are theoretically calculated for any Knudsen number. Investigation of the new model's performance shows that it accurately reproduces thermal transpiration at both low and high Knudsen numbers, an achievement not previously possible with the conventional 13-moment closure system. Comparison of the new uniform gas model with the direct simulation Monte Carlo method reveals that it significantly outperforms traditional uniform gas models in simulating thermal transpiration at the canonical level, particularly in the regime of thermal transpiration's saturation. This study aims to contribute a novel approach for modeling thermal transpiration in rarefied micro-flows.

This paper proposes a novel approach to few-shot semantic parsing that leverages
large-scale, unannotated text data in combination with a small set of seed
examples. A generated semantic parser, trained jointly with a language model, is
optimized through maximum likelihood estimation within the framework of self-supervised
learning. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this approach on datasets
from the Microsoft Semantic Parsing Benchmark and the Long Logical Forms Corpus,
and also include analysis of its performance under increasing few-shot settings.

The High Energy Physics community's existing active pixel sensor and low gain avalanche diode technologies approach their practical technological limits due to the constraints imposed by thin silicon interaction layers. To alleviate this, the LHCb upgrade initiative has spearheaded novel thin semiconductor technologies. Two promising options were investigated by CERN's electronics group: the Depleted Monolithic Active Pixel Sensor and the low gain avalanche diode with alternating charge coupling, both of which enable very thin depletion regions, around 50 micrometers, allowing for increased z-position resolution. In this study, sensor characteristics and initial performance assessments are detailed alongside laboratory-level investigations of range and stop processes on a DMAPS, with a focus on its potential in particle identification applications. A comprehensive analysis of both sensor types was conducted at the single hit level using a 20 TeV proton-proton collision dataset recorded by the LHCb detector, utilizing the full calibration capabilities of its upgrade scheme. Additionally, the dataset enabled the evaluation of the impact of sensor types on track length reconstruction precision.

Using the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory's X-ray Telescope and the European Space Agency's XMM-Newton, we conducted a comprehensive, multi-wavelength observation of the low-mass AGN 2XMM J123103.2+110648 (J1231). This simultaneous observation revealed a complex X-ray spectrum characterized by strong Fe K$\alpha$ fluorescence lines, iron absorption, and possibly narrow soft Fe lines. Spectral analysis showed X-ray emission originating from an accretion disk surrounded by a broad ionized region, consistent with previous observations. Moreover, the J1231 source exhibited a two-stage X-ray variability pattern: rapid, high-amplitude fluctuations in the soft X-ray band (0.2-2 keV) and moderate hard X-ray (2-10 keV) fluctuations. Notably, the J1231 source's low X-ray luminosity ($\sim$10$^{41}$ erg s$^{-1}$) makes it a rare low-luminosity AGN. Our spectral analysis and models suggest X-ray emission is produced by the Comptonization of soft photons from the accretion disk within the ionized accretion disk corona. Notably, the J1231 source's X-ray variability and spectra share similarities with those seen in high accretion rate AGNs.

We've conducted a groundbreaking study of B-type magnetic stars in the Large Magellanic Cloud, specifically examining their subdwarf B counterparts, and discovered an intriguing connection to the existence of magnetic fields in subdwarf B binary systems. Our findings indicate that the magnetic fields surrounding these subdwarf B stars can be attributed to a magnetohydrodynamic process, and the occurrence rate of magnetic fields in LMC subdwarf B binary systems is significantly influenced by the temporal and spatial aspects of star formation.

This study utilizes oscillator operators as intertwining tools in one dimension, drawing on existing literature to develop a methodical framework centered around a core concept of interconnection. By leveraging this approach, we successfully construct solutions involving hydrogen-like systems in two and three dimensions, as well as harmonic oscillators in one, two, and three dimensional spaces.

We studied nine galaxies with low oxygen abundance (below solar levels) and analyzed their dust properties using 100-micron and 160-micron flux measurements from the Spitzer Infrared Survey Science Archive. By employing the Starlight code, we modeled the star formation rates and stellar masses based on their ultraviolet and optical data, while taking the dust properties into account. Our analysis revealed that in these galaxies, the star formation rates derived from infrared data differed significantly from those based on H-beta and H30α data, and that their dust characteristics also varied significantly, indicating a clear separation from solar metallicity galaxies in the color-magnitude plane. Moreover, it was evident that these galaxies could not be accurately described by a black-body dust emission, and when compared to a black body with the same luminosity, their 160-micron emission was underluminous, and they exhibited reduced dust masses relative to their stellar masses compared to S0 galaxies and star-forming galaxies at solar metallicity. We hypothesize that these galaxies may have unique properties, such as a dust-free component or a two-component dust population with unique color characteristics, and suggest that they represent a new class of galaxies with infrared characteristics, which may have been overlooked in previous studies.

We exhibit an infinite dihedral group as the sole virtually cyclic group that admits an adaptable, minimal, and non-trivial flow on a smooth manifold as a topological group action. This finding contrasts sharply with the behavior observed in other virtually cyclic groups with co-infinite and non-trivial flows having minimal points, as characterized by Looi and Rafal.

In this research, several aspects of why kernel-driven techniques can efficiently and accurately solve mathematical problems using an infinite number of variables are explored. It becomes clear that the use of advanced techniques to sample data points and sophisticated kernel selection methods which adapt to specific problems significantly improves the efficiency and speed of these techniques. Furthermore, our research shows that kernel-based techniques often outperform traditional methods like Galerkin approaches in terms of convergence and can even solve complex and irregular problems that are inapplicable to classical techniques. Lastly, our research proposes a technique to determine the optimal size of kernel-driven networks that solves mathematical problems to a specified level of approximation without the need for excessive computational resources. The effectiveness of this technique is demonstrated through a series of case studies on mathematical problems that have been solved both analytically using kernel-driven networks and numerically using traditional methods. These studies also reveal the potential of integrating kernel-driven techniques with other techniques to create powerful hybrid algorithms for solving mathematical problems that have low levels of convergence or are computationally expensive to solve using traditional methods.

This architecture paper introduces a novel observer design for estimating the state of complex systems such as deterministic epidemic models, multi-agent systems, power distribution networks, and building control systems. The theory behind state estimation in dynamic systems dates back to the 1960s with the creation of the Kalman filter in 1960. Since then, various observer architectures have been developed for nonlinear systems, including Luenberger-type observers, high-gain observers, sliding mode observers, and adaptive observers, all of which enable accurate state estimation from output measurements. The proposed architecture unifies these concepts to efficiently estimate the state of intricate nonlinear systems like those modeling epidemics. By leveraging the proposed architecture, sensor failures in epidemic models can be detected and isolated using estimated residual errors. The paper showcases the practical application of the proposed observer architecture in real-world scenarios, demonstrating its efficacy in estimating the state of an SIR epidemic model under noisy conditions.

Temporal knowledge graphs and their corresponding embeddings are crucial components
in data integration tasks involving multiple databases. Currently, most approaches
to temporal KG embeddings fail to effectively incorporate and utilize temporal
information within our proposed framework, FastTime. Fastime efficiently captures
and models temporal patterns in the background by utilizing temporal language
elements, thereby addressing a significant gap in the existing approaches. The
evaluation results indicate that our method significantly outperforms the current
state-of-the-art approaches in terms of temporal KG embeddings, with a notable 5x
improvement in runtime compared to the best existing method.

For single-mode Kerr-lens mode-locking to occur stably in a laser system, there needs to be a precise balance between dispersion and nonlinearities. Achieving this equilibrium often necessitates access to diverse materials, which can have diverse properties. In our work, we demonstrate multi-cycle Kerr-lens mode-locking within a laser that is nearly linearly dispersed, employing only two types of materials: highly non-linear silicon and passive graphite sheets. This is initially possible due to silicon's high nonlinear coefficient, which compensates for its low dispersion loss, combined with graphite's role in providing the necessary positive dispersion during mode-locking initiation. This approach to understanding and stabilizing Kerr-lens mode-locking is characterized within a unified theoretical model that is supported by experimental outcomes.

In asynchronous federated online learning, a server hosts a model and conducts training sessions with a model host.
Existing research on asynchronous federated learning has focused on issues such as stale client participation and resource constraints, often assuming synchronous sessions and clients with full model capabilities.
This paper presents a new approach, PSHARE-FOL, that improves communication efficiency in asynchronous sessions by enabling clients to share only necessary model parts.
Through theoretical analysis, we show that the PSHARE-FOL algorithm offers an average regret of $\tilde{O}(K^{\frac{3}{4}}H^{\frac{1}{2}})$.
Experiments demonstrate that PSHARE-FOL outperforms existing methods in both communication efficiency and model accuracy.

We present the optical absorption characteristics of thin silicon films paired with a photonic crystal back reflector, measured over the 1500--800 nm wavelength range. By adjusting the thickness of the silicon films, we were able to tune and observe distinct regions of high absorption within the photonic crystal's forbidden band, resulting in absorptivity values exceeding 0.9 within a very narrow bandwidth, as narrow as 50 nm. Furthermore, our experiments show that increasing the pitch-to-period ratio within the photonic crystal's honeycomb structure expands the forbidden band's width, concurrently decreasing the associated pass bands' widths.

Two specific functions, defined by the recursive relationships $f_{odd}(z) = \sqrt{e^{f_{even}(z)^2} - 1}$ and $f_{even}(z) = \sqrt{e^{f_{odd}(z)^2} + 1}$, serve as inverse functions to the exponential map within certain regions of the complex plane. Multiple such regions exist, corresponding to different branch choices. We investigate how these functions behave under the influence of the exponential map and develop formal power series expansions, enabling us to accurately portray their characteristics near poles and within a specified domain. We also provide numerical evidence supporting our findings regarding the behavior of these functions across various regions of the complex plane.

We suggest a novel class of structures, high dimensional expanders (HDEs), which we believe will have various applications in the field of RCPC. This study primarily focuses on the theorems related to HDEs in theoretical computer science, specifically on how these structures can lead to the creation of locally decodable codes, providing evidence for their existence.

The structure of GdInO$_3$ is composed of perovskite units arranged in an orthorhombic, tilted lattice containing Gd$^{3+}$ ions in sites with local C$_{2v}$ symmetry. Neutron inelastic scattering experiments were conducted at two temperatures while the sample was placed in a magnetic field aligned along the local C$_2$ axis of each site. Inelastic losses were detected with sufficient intensity, and analysis revealed the presence of localized magnetic excitations associated with individual Gd$^{3+}$ ions as well as lower energy collective spin wave excitations.

In various real-world sparse networks, many nodes share similarities in their connections and thus benefit from combining their feature sets. We introduce the Sum of Normalized Higher-order Adjacency Matrix approach to represent nodes by integrating neighboring information from the sparse network, increasing data points to improve learning potential in a given domain. Experimental results from recommending the Next Item in Netflix-style film recommendations using MovieLens data, and Facebook friend suggestion using Geographicham data, demonstrate the proposed SNHAM's effectiveness under realistic conditions in recommending the next item.

A value-added analytical technique for characterizing liquid pills composed of multiple solvents involves Raman spectroscopy. To enhance the signal, we've developed a specialized two-room setup that activates the pill by heating it up quickly, and subsequently collects a strong signal from the space above it. Our research focuses on investigating the dynamics of pill heating, which we've done using high-speed imaging and spectroscopy. Furthermore, we've achieved accurate simulations of these vapor dynamics through the use of the DISCUS code, which revealed that the introduction of a customized, curved baffle in the reaction chamber significantly prolongs the lifetime of the desired vapor and隐匿s unwanted particles.

A mathematical method is presented to convert a mathematical model of an optical communication system into an efficient computational algorithm. This approach utilizes software tools capable of interpreting differential equations and performing numerical analysis to generate a computational algorithm that can be executed on modern computer hardware. A nonlinear optical system model is employed as a case study to demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, resulting in a significant reduction in the time required for a system simulation, from days to hours. This efficient algorithm also allows for the development of both feed-forward and feedback equalizers that leverage prior knowledge of system nonlinearities. Moreover, a simplified version of the algorithm is explored to diagnose polarization-multiplexed formats and identify the structure of optical signals.

The application of infrared and visible light imagery in fire safety is growing due to their distinct capabilities. This paper introduces a new method called Deep Learning-based Image Fusion, which combines Infrared Thermal and Visible Light Images to create a single, enhanced image that is more informative and visually appealing. This novel strategy surpasses traditional image fusion techniques by significantly reducing the rate of incorrect detections, making it ideal for high-stakes environments. By utilizing deep learning, the proposed technique outperforms other fusion methods while also showcasing its potential through quantitative and qualitative assessments in a real-world fire scenario.

Diagnosing mental health conditions on social media is an emerging application of NLP.
Existing studies have often applied machine learning models to diagnose mental health
disorders from social media data.
However, there has been a lack of in-depth model analysis, and the findings have yet to
be thoroughly evaluated.
This paper presents a model that uses BERT and ensemble learning techniques to
aid in the diagnosis of mental health conditions on social media.
We utilize data from multiple sources, such as Reddit and Twitter, and employ a
cross-validation approach.
The results indicate that our NLP-based ensemble model can be as effective as
clinical models in predicting depression, with a 91.1% test accuracy.
Moreover, our findings demonstrate that the proposed ensemble model outperforms
existing models in classifying mental health conditions on Twitter and Reddit.
Additionally, our study highlights the strengths and limitations of our model,
along with suggestions for future research and potential applications.

This research introduces a novel discrete-time deterministic model, specifically designed for actions in discrete-time for effectively managing SARS-CoV-19 vaccination efforts. By employing optimal control theory, our model allocates limited hospital resources to isolate infected patients and contain the spread of SARS-CoV-19 within the community. Furthermore, our study validates the necessity of combining lockdown measures with the actions taken by hospitals and health care institutions. Simulation outcomes indicate that: (i) hospitals' or clinics' findings, when paired with lockdown measures, can either contain the epidemic or lead to its defeat; (ii) clinics' findings alone may not be sufficient to prevent the epidemic from spreading, as evidenced by the presence of infected patients at the end of the process.

Theoretical studies of nuclear resonance interactions have a practical local application.
A recent study focused on the energy overlap between the Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance and the Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance using a computational model.
A specific calculation model, combining the Isoscalar Giant Quadrupole Resonance and Isoscalar Giant Monopole Resonance, was used on a set of deformed nuclei from calcium to lead.
The results showed that the interaction significantly redistributes the energy, with the most pronounced red shifts occurring at moderate quadrupole deformations.
A model-based analysis of coupling processes and their quantification showed strong correlations with nuclear deformation.
The findings from this study are supported by previous studies, including those using different methodologies.

This research explores the impact of a static friction area in open-loop and closed-loop dynamics, focusing on the characteristics of the motion steady state. The article examines the characteristics of the motion half-cycle length function in the presence of an static friction area and evaluates the stability of the motion steady state. The analysis extends to the case where system parameters and forces are subject to uncertainty.

Effective decision-making tools for financial investors are increasingly reliant on machine learning, with trading strategies being automatically developed and tested through backtesting in a risk-free simulated environment.  However, the accuracy of the learned strategies can be compromised when transaction costs and market liquidity are not factored in during the backtesting process.  To address this limitation, a new approach uses machine learning to analyze historical market data in conjunction with simulated trading simulations that incorporate the effects of transaction costs and order execution processes into the overall strategy.  By incorporating these trading frictions into the learning process, the strategies developed perform consistently across various market conditions and time periods.

In recent years, deep learning-based recommendation systems have significantly improved user engagement. However, user experience can still be compromised if recommendations don't align with user intent. Existing sequential recommendation systems provide a framework for optimizing user experience but struggle to capture complex user intent in real-world applications. This paper presents the first application of transformer-based architecture in sequential recommendation to enhance user experience and thus, improve overall user experience through multi-faceted intent representation learning. By utilizing a transformer model to accurately capture complex user behavior, it becomes possible to represent both explicit user intent and implicit associations. While the intent representation model achieves state-of-the-art performance on benchmark datasets, its effectiveness in real-world settings, such as Alibaba's, remains to be verified. Consequently, we've developed a multi-stage intent learning framework that balances inference speed and overall performance, utilizing both online and offline training data to ensure accurate user intent estimation. Our framework achieves state-of-the-art performance on Alibaba's benchmark dataset, surpassing existing baseline models in various metrics.

In this research, a reduced form of the conflineral Heun equation with two singular points is analyzed.  A holomorphic solution to this  reducible equation exists in the complex plane for specific values of two parameters.  By applying a transformation, we derive a new series expansion for the parameters and determine its reduced form, yielding a power series with an infinite radius of convergence. Furthermore, we establish a power-law asymptotic expansion for the solution behavior at large values of the parameters and investigate a corresponding power series with an infinite radius of convergence.

This study investigates low-rank matrix recovery and PCA, using a weighted combination of data and focusing on the impact of outliers. Outliers can be modeled as perturbations to a matrix's columns, and our goal is to understand how these deviations affect PCA when performing a weighted combination of data. This research provides a novel bound on the alignment between PCA on combined data and PCA on its underlying matrix, demonstrating the robustness of PCA on combined data even in the presence of outliers. This outcome reveals that weighted combinations can enhance PCA's performance in outlier-prone scenarios, a phenomenon not previously explained through the lens of outlier detection and analysis.

Our research involves discovering topologically non-trivial states localized at boundaries in a wide variety of systems, extending beyond quantum frameworks and high-dimensional systems like classical arrays of coupled harmonic oscillators. We uncover that 1D classical systems without kinetic energy need not exhibit symmetry to show states of fractional boundary modes. These unique states have remained largely unexplored due to their presence being obscured by inherent thermodynamic instabilities in such systems. Moreover, we demonstrate the existence of these 1D classical systems at boundaries within higher-dimensional harmonic oscillator arrays, thereby expanding the known phase diagrams of these systems to show 1D localized modes at corners and edges with topological invariants. These findings reveal that 1D topological states are far more widespread and prevalent than initially thought across both classical and non-quantum frameworks.

For the $\mathrm{B}$ meson transitions into $\phi$, $\rho$, $J/\psi$, and other vector mesons, as well as lepton pairs, existing experiments are primarily sensitive to a few decay pathways. Conversely, future experiments such as LHCb, CDF2, LHC, and LHCa will be able to explore additional decay channels by reconstructing the other half of the decay process involving unobserved vector mesons using its decay products. Since these vector mesons decay into readily observable particles like pions or muons at the LHC, it becomes feasible to obtain statistically significant data on several decay pathways in a single experiment. Furthermore, it is anticipated that very small signals may become detectable. The novel capability to record these "golden" decay pathways will significantly boost the potential for detecting deviations in several key observables from the Standard Model predictions, specifically for the transitions $\mathrm{B} \to \ell\ell$ where $\ell$ represents light particles such as muons or electrons. Specifically, measurements of branching fractions for the transitions $\mathrm{B} \to \ell\ell$ will benefit greatly, with potential sensitivity improvements of two orders of magnitude for the $\mathrm{B} \to \ell\ell$ pathway where $\ell$ is a muon.

In networked systems, ensuring a stable and robust controller amidst changing network conditions is a significant challenge. To address this, we utilize an optimal network scheduling algorithm by Bass that enhances both stability and resilience. By maintaining a stable queue, Bass' algorithm allows the controller to efficiently process measurements and control actions with minimal delay. Building on this concept, we develop a modified algorithm, named ConAlg, which applies to continuous-time linear systems with varying network states. Conard ensures exponential system stability while achieving minimum control energy through the use of a novel feedback control strategy. A proposed projection feedback mechanism ensures strong stability of the closed-loop system despite state changes. Furthermore, by considering measurement and control action delays, we develop a time-varying feedback controller through Lyapunov analysis and optimize energy usage. Numerical examples demonstrate ConAlg's performance advantages.

This study introduces a universal AI framework for analyzing brain magnetic resonance images to detect Alzheimer's disease and mild cognitive impairment. This framework integrates multiple advanced deep learning techniques, including automatic image segmentation, feature extraction, and classification. Using established public datasets from the AdMIRAL and LME datasets, we evaluated the developed framework and monitored its general applicability through a rigorous cross-validation approach. Our clinical AI framework achieved impressive performance metrics of 91% and 94% accuracy and area under the curve respectively, on the validation data. Furthermore, we trained and tested distinct convolutional neural network architectures, each producing distinct image feature maps with significantly different spatial resolutions and texture patterns. This study successfully demonstrated the feasibility of using the proposed framework for automatic detection of cognitive impairment in brain MRI images.

This code contributes a useful tool to the field of complex network research, specifically focusing on the study of networks with continuous and time-varying dynamics through their linear stability analysis. By extending previous research on static networks, we have developed a flexible analytical framework capable of handling various network configurations, including random and small-world topologies, and signal-based and state-based coupling mechanisms. Additionally, the framework allows for fast computation of eigendirections and system states, and can easily accommodate changes in network topology and system parameters.

This study examines an adaptive dynamics model to understand how ecological and evolutionary changes interact over long time periods. The model considers stochastic ecological fluctuations and environmental changes influenced by temperature and mutation sensitivity. Different values of these factors can shift the system from isolated processes to an intertwined complex or a system with distinct separation of time scales. Specifically, at high sensitivity and low environmental variability, ecological and evolutionary echelons merge and potentially enter a critical state at critical temperature.

This paper examines how speech representation models are affected by attacks from adversaries with varying levels of information access and provides a comparative analysis of their vulnerabilities. Three distinct types of attacks on speech models are discussed: an adversary with access to the target model's labels, an adversary with prior knowledge of the target model and its labels, and an adversary with limited prior knowledge. Our results reveal that speech models are particularly susceptible to attacks from adversaries with different levels of information access and indicate that defenses developed to be robust against these attacks can be manipulated to be less resistant to others. Consequently, we suggest that the evaluation of speech representation models should include a comparison of their resistance to various attacks in order to achieve a more accurate assessment of their security resilience.

Among Decentralized Finance models, Automated Market Makers are the most prevalent type. They feature order books modeled after piecewise functions, where the curve's monotonicity and convexity in the price axis ensure the orchestration of order execution. We investigate the implications of this model in a market saturated with orders. We demonstrate through theoretical analysis that the curvature of the curve set by the Automated Market Maker significantly influences the investor experience, order execution speed, and potential for arbitrage opportunities. We develop an optimal strategy that takes into account this curvature, maximizing the investor's return. We also introduce a general framework for evaluating optimal execution strategies that can be applied to any type of curve.

This study proposes an odds ratio-based causal robustness framework applicable to binary outcomes and exposures with missing data, utilizing an adapted single-world intervention graph to evaluate potential causal conclusions' robustness in the absence of complete data. Building on the missing-at-random property, the framework introduces an E-value to measure a causal conclusion's robustness when data is incomplete, showcasing that as additional data is gathered with a completely randomized method for collecting data, the E-value decreases, signifying increased robustness. Applying this to a specific scenario, the framework was applied to determine whether an intervention aiming to reduce obesity would lead to decreased depressive symptoms. Analyzing available data via ordinary least squares and difference-in-discontinuity estimates indicated the existence of a causal relationship, an outcome sustained when data missingness followed random sampling. However, when considering potential biases from missing data, this causal relationship was found to be robust only when an odds ratio effect size was considered but not when a linear relationship was assumed.

Two $U_q(\sl_2)$-algebra actions on the quantum plane are presented, both exhibiting $U_q(\sl_2)$ symmetry in a way that can be transformed into a standard form via an automorphism of $U_q(\sl_2)$. The two actions are not equivalent, but can be related through an automorphism of $U_q(\sl_2)$, indicating that $U_q(\sl_2)$ actions on the quantum plane are parameterized by a parameter (taking values of 0 or 1) related to an automorphism of $U_q(\sl_2)$.

The integration of Blockchain technology in Internet of Vehicles (IoV) systems has significant potential, addressing several of their current limitations. This study provides a comprehensive analysis of IoV's key applications and the primary challenges they face, as well as their solution through the implementation of Blockchain. Focusing on data security, privacy, and energy efficiency, this study examines the applicability of various Blockchain variants, such as directed consensus mechanisms, lightweight encryption methods, and intelligent contract techniques, in enhancing Iov's functionality. The study's outcome contributes to further research and development in this field.

Measurements are made of the fragmentation probability of high-energy colorful particles into specific types of strange mesons.  To achieve this, a sample of B mesons containing a particular unstable particle, decaying into a lone kaon and other products, is analyzed.  To obtain the required information, other B mesons with a similar decay pattern are used.  By using various methods and statistics, precise estimates are obtained for high-energy particles that transform into J/psi kaon pairs and semileptonic decay products.  Results indicate that high-energy charm particles are more likely to transform into certain types of strange mesons than their counterparts, but these rates align within the range of predicted uncertainty levels.  Furthermore, these rates exhibit similar patterns across various momentum frames.  By examining certain decays of high-energy particles that produce leptons and other products, an understanding of theoretical predictions is achieved.  To achieve this, precise calculations and statistical analysis are carried out, resulting in precise estimates of high-energy particles that transform into J/psi muon and kaon decay products.

We've started designing a cryogenic platform featuring a 2T DC SQUID reader, 
SGBT reader, XGUN reader and single-photon detector that will aid the 
development of large-scale experiments on quantum matter. 
Considering past experiments' requirements, we've created a 1.05 x 0.8 
x 0.82 meter experiment volume, and we're aiming to integrate multiple 
experiment elements, thereby enabling the investigation of various quantum 
matter issues. This cryogenic platform's design and its possible 
applications are described in detail in this paper.

In cryptography, ensuring security relies on following best practices, which can be difficult due to the high level of technical expertise required to identify and avoid mistakes. To address this, several advanced crypto libraries have been developed across various languages such as Python, Java, and C, which provide standardized interfaces to cryptographic algorithms. Despite this, we discovered through an in-depth analysis that Python's crypto modules are inherently more complicated and unclear than their Java and C counterparts, which might contribute to higher rates of crypto-related errors. Our investigation, which included a close review of Python, Java, and C code, as well as a study of security flaws and software testing, revealed that the API design in Python is less intuitive and more difficult to use compared to Java and C. As a result, our findings suggest that developers are more likely to use Python's crypto modules correctly when given explicit guidance or automated assistance, which highlights the importance of creating more intuitive and simpler crypto interfaces to improve software security.

This work presents an efficient approach to processing a vast amount of image data, including extrinsic, intrinsic, and 3D object information, from multiple perspectives. As we increase the camera count and object database size to tens of thousands, our methods achieve near-perfect recovery of camera positions and internal dimensions, while effectively processing intrinsic unknowns within a reasonable timeframe. Notably, our technique demonstrates scalability in large-scale scenarios, where the volume of object data may become a limiting factor. Additionally, our methods have successfully recovered the geometric and textual properties of diverse architectural structures across a vast knowledge base.

To obtain a detailed view of subsurface geological structures, researchers are using seismic data sparse synthesis to recover geological coefficients efficiently. A novel model has been developed, featuring a non-convex and non-uniform synthesis operator, offering more flexibility in reflecting coefficients and robustness against errors in the reference data. By co-sparsifying the data and subsampling seismic traces, the new model reduces computational complexity while improving resolution and robustness. Extensive testing has been conducted in controlled settings and with real-world data, consistently demonstrating the superior performance of the new model compared to traditional sparse synthesis methods.

In this research, we investigate the compactness of an integral operator, $T_g$, on BMOA_{p} for $1 < p < 2$, and determine that $T_g$ is a compact operator on this space if and only if $T_g$ operates in a weakly compact manner within BMOA_{p} under certain conditions involving specific mathematical expressions involving limits of $g'$ in bounded subsets of BMOA_{p}.

Our research focuses on developing quantum algorithms to calculate conformal data from low-energy overlaps in quantum spin chains, presenting a specific strategy for calculating the central charge without relying on the finite size scaling method and instead utilizing the eigenstates of the open Heisenberg chain's transfer matrix. Furthermore, we extend this approach to a unique method for extracting conformal data from the finite size scaling of energy spectra and suggest its applicability within a quantum computer's context. This study demonstrates significant potential in leveraging quantum computers for determining CFT data in a variety of quantum systems.

A novel set-valued tagging approach is proposed for part-of-speech (PoS) tagging, enabling the generation of multiple valid tag sequences. We demonstrate that set-valued tagging results in superior accuracy for word-based taggers, particularly when encountering unknown words. Building upon an existing Bayesian inference algorithm, a new Markov chain (MCMC) tagging algorithm is developed. We also introduce a consensus-based method for producing single tag sequences from those generated by the MCMC tagger, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy on the Penn Treebank dataset at the level of valid sequences.

This study focuses on the implications of uniform convergence for a sequence of demand functions within a compact set of price-wealth combinations, particularly when the limit has non-negative price and non-negative wealth components. We demonstrate that if the sequence of continuous, strictly concave, monotone preferences gives rise to uniformly convergent demand functions, then the limit will also be a continuously differentiable, strictly concave, monotone preference with a corresponding demand function that exhibits specific properties related to elasticity and the Allen-Haefler index. Conversely, preferences with constant elasticity of demand give rise to demand functions belonging to the uniformly convergent class. We present a corresponding result regarding Aggregative Preferences, characterized by demands exhibiting additive properties analogous to Vind's condition.

As urban areas grow increasingly complex due to the incorporation of advanced technology and infrastructure, they are evolving into intelligent city systems that streamline the flow of information and resources such as energy and water. Despite the advantages brought about by smart city initiatives, they often struggle to translate human-specified goals and constraints into technical terms, resulting in systems with ambiguous or inaccurate specifications. To address this challenge, monitoring systems in smart cities need to adapt to handle evolving requirements and integrate multiple data sources to provide a comprehensive understanding of system status. This study presents a monitoring system design for smart cities that incorporates an adaptable rule engine that can learn and adapt to changing circumstances and integrate data from diverse sensors and models to create a real-time, technical system view. Using the knowledge that smart city systems aim to enhance overall system health, our adaptive rule engine can refine technical models and improve the accuracy of system monitoring. We demonstrate the developed system through a case study of a sustainable smart campus, focusing on specific requirements like energy efficiency and water conservation.

Variational Quantum Algorithms are one of the primary candidates for the ultimate utilization of quantum devices due to their iterative nature. Quantum computers can find approximate solutions to certain problems more efficiently than classical computers through these algorithms. A recent candidate in this class is the Variational Quantum Eigensolver algorithm, which has the potential to simulate quantum systems on quantum computers. The VECS algorithm's performance in the presence of noise has yet to be extensively studied, and in this research, we analyze how different parameters affect its performance in noisy quantum circuits simulating the ground states of $H_2$ molecules. We found that mitigating noise in the VQE algorithm comes at a significant cost in terms of convergence rate and memory requirements. However, mitigating noise can be feasible if the noise simulating the quantum gate is already in place or if there's a substantial overhead in not mitigating noise.

Given a stable functor $F\colon E\to E'$ between groff categories with accessible monadic ideals, the result is that $F$ stably preserves quotient maps, the isomorphism isomorphism theorem applies, and E'/E is equivalent to the category of chains. This leads to the conclusion that any topos with suprema of chain-based access, the n-permutable regular category has suprema of chain-based access, the n-topos with suprema of chain-based access has stable totality, and the biaccessible n-topos with suprema of chain-based access has stable biorthogonality.

This novel method evaluates spatial correlations between extreme weather events by examining high winds or the Strongest Surface Wind event (SSWE) patterns seen over the North Atlantic Ocean. By analyzing data collected between 1991 and 2016 from modern meteorological satellites, the research reveals how extremal correlations in wind speeds and wave heights persist across various distances across the region, whereas significant wind shear events exhibit a rapid decay after a characteristic scale of 250km. The findings suggest that extreme weather patterns change significantly with altitude, with extreme behavior observed at lower levels not necessarily correlating with that at upper levels.

We introduce CLIP-TextCLIP, an enhanced CLIP model utilizing a pre-trained language model to refine CLIP's image embeddings through text embeddings. To achieve this, we employ CLIP's vision encoder as the text encoder in CLIP-TextCLIP. Specifically, we incorporate CLIP's visual encoder to improve the CLIP-TextCLIP model by TextCLIP-Vision-Guided Texts (TextCLIP-VGTs). TextCLIP-VGTs are generated by CLIP-TextCLip using CLIP's vision encoder as the text CLIP-TextCLIP attention map, with subsequent refinement by the CLIP-TextCLIP model. This process enables CLIP-TextCLip to further refine CLIP-TextCLip's image embedding, thereby boosting the semantic correlation between CLIP-TextCLip images and texts. This research is motivated by the challenge of finding improved ways to estimate the inverse of details from noisy, additional data, for information rich observations. We establish a general framework for shifting noisy, additional data before applying a basic estimator, focusing on both theoretical optimality and practical applicability. We demonstrate that under noises which are symmetric, the optimal direction for this shift is along the gradients of loss functions. However, when noises are asymmetric, there's no clear optimal direction and often a zero shift is preferred. A theoretical shift bound helps us understand the value of this shift procedure and its implications. We also show the framework's value through real-world examples, focusing on relative entropy and of of norms, and its limitations when dealing with the absolute value of norms.

MacKay functors hold significant significance in stable homotopy theory and are studied within the framework of double categories to provide a unified approach. By leveraging this perspective, we delve into various aspects of stable homotopy theory and Mackey functors, including their role in reflecting the homotopy limit. This is achieved through a notion of weak functors in the category of G-spectra, which we demonstrate to preserve Mackey functors. Consequently, this allows us to establish an equivalence between Mackey functors and G-spectra's homotopy theory. Furthermore, this framework enables the translation of important constructions, such as smashing products and Smith theories, from the language of Mackey functors.

Let $R$ be a commutative unital ring, and let $I$ be a $\mathfrak{p}$-primary ideal, where $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime ideal in $R$. This work presents four methods to compute the zero submodule of the local cohomology module, namely, ${\rm coh}_I(R)$, without relying on an explicit Iwasawa structure theorem for this module. These approaches result in a character function $\theta\colon\mathbb{N}^{\frak{p}/\mathfrak{q}}\to\mathbb{Z}$, where $\mathfrak{q}=\bigcap_{\mathfrak{m}\supseteq\mathfrak{p}}\mathfrak{m}$ is the radical of $I$ with $\mathfrak{m}$ ranging over the maximal ideals containing $I$. Furthermore, this function can be used to determine whether the $I$-local cohomology module of $R$ is $\mathbb{Z}$-free. One of these methods involves generalizing the Zibrulevici-Herzog-Shimada module to equidimensional, equicodimensional, and formally equidimensional Noetherian rings $R$ that are non-necessarily commutative, under the condition of $I$ being an ideal that is $\mathfrak{p}$-primary.
